reusable_risk_records.risk_name: Implicit coercion changes the value being compared or combined
reusable_risk_records.plain_language_description: A comparison, arithmetic operation, string concatenation, or truthiness check relies on JavaScript converting a value first.
failure_consequences: Numeric operation produces NaN or a string
Branch executes for a value the reader expected to be false
diagnostic_prompts: List every ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=, +, Boolean(), if, ||, &&, ?? and template/string conversion site.
Check object-to-primitive hooks such as valueOf(), toString(), Symbol.toPrimitive when objects participate in operators.
preferred_mitigations: Prefer explicit conversion near the boundary.
Prefer ===/!== unless the loose comparison is intentional and documented.
Add tests for numeric strings, empty strings, 0, false, null, undefined, NaN, and objects.

reusable_risk_records.plain_language_description: A variable may be null or undefined before a property read, element read, method call, destructuring step, or function invocation.
failure_consequences: Optional chaining hides a missing required value

Use ?. only when absence is an accepted outcome.
Preserve distinction between null and undefined when APIs depend on it.

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: JavaScript has two nullish values: one commonly used to mean intentional absence and one commonly produced when a value has not been assigned or a property is missing.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: null is a language value denoting no object. undefined is the value of uninitialized variables, missing parameters, and absent object properties. They compare loosely equal to each other but are distinct under strict equality.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: null, undefined, value == null, value === undefined, parameter defaults, property reads
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Most property-access crashes begin as a nullish-state modeling problem. The distinction also affects JSON, defaults, APIs, and optional chaining.
common_use: Distinguish absent property from present null value
common_misuse: Using || when null/undefined must be distinguished from 0, empty string, or false
Treating optional chaining as proof a required value exists
Serializing and expecting undefined properties to survive JSON
debugging_symptoms: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined/null
Branch takes fallback for valid falsy value
API receives null where omitted argument was intended
safe_refactor_notes: Keep nullish guards near property access
When replacing guards with ?., ensure absence is acceptable
Preserve public API distinction in refactors

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Conditionals do not require booleans; JavaScript converts many values to true or false in Boolean contexts.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: Falsy values include false, 0, -0, 0n where applicable, empty string, null, undefined, and NaN. Other ordinary object values are truthy. Boolean conversion is used by if, while, !, &&, ||, and the conditional operator.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: if (value), !value, value && expr, value || fallback, Boolean(value)
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Truthiness is compact but can collapse distinct states such as empty string, zero, missing value, and false.
common_use: Check presence only when all falsy values mean absent
common_misuse: Using if (count) when zero is valid
Using value || fallback for empty string or 0
Assuming [] or {} are falsy
tests_or_checks: Create tests for 0, "", false, null, undefined, NaN, [], {}
Prefer value != null for nullish-only checks
safe_refactor_notes: Do not replace explicit comparisons with truthiness unless all falsy values are equivalent
Document sentinel values

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Functions can be stored, passed, returned, and invoked like other values.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: Function declarations, function expressions, and arrow functions create callable objects. Functions may have properties, close over scope, and differ in this/arguments/new behavior.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: function f(){}, const f = function(){}, const f = x => x, callback(fn)
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Callbacks, higher-order APIs, modules, and event handlers depend on functions as first-class values.
common_use: Store behavior in objects or maps
common_misuse: Invoking when a reference is needed
Passing this-dependent method without binding
Assuming arrow and function are interchangeable
debugging_symptoms: Function cannot be used as constructor
tests_or_checks: Check this, arguments, and new requirements
safe_refactor_notes: Preserve function form when this/arguments/constructor behavior matters
Name functions when stack traces matter

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: A function can remember variables from the lexical scope where it was created.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: Nested functions and returned callbacks retain access to outer lexical bindings. They observe the variable binding, not an automatic deep snapshot of every value.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: function outer(){ let x=0; return () => ++x; }

Capturing mutable loop/state by accident
Leaking memory through long-lived closures over large objects

safe_refactor_notes: Pass explicit parameters when snapshot is intended
Reset closure state in test setup
Avoid capturing broad objects unnecessarily

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: The value of this depends on how a function is invoked, not only where it is defined.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: Method calls set this to the receiver. Plain function calls, constructor calls, call/apply/bind, event callbacks, and arrow functions differ. Arrow functions capture lexical this and cannot be used as ordinary methods requiring dynamic this.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: obj.m(), f(), new C(), f.call(obj), f.bind(obj), () => this.x
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: this bugs are uniquely common in methods, callbacks, classes, event handlers, and extracted functions.

common_misuse: Passing obj.method directly as callback
Using arrow for prototype method needing receiver
Forgetting strict-mode plain-call this

tests_or_checks: Identify every this use and invocation form
safe_refactor_notes: Refactor methods to arrows only when receiver semantics are irrelevant
Bind at construction or call boundary, not randomly inside logic

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: JavaScript class syntax is modern syntax over prototype-based objects.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: class declarations define constructor functions and prototype methods. Instance state is initialized in constructors or fields. Inheritance uses prototype chains and super. Class bodies are strict.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: class C { constructor(x){ this.x=x } method(){} } new C(1)
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Class syntax improves readability but does not erase prototype, this, or object-reference semantics.
common_use: Use subclassing where substitutability is clear
common_misuse: Assuming class methods are copied per instance
Using instance arrow fields for every method without memory/identity reason
Treating private state, prototype methods, and closures as identical
debugging_symptoms: Subclass method cannot access super as expected
safe_refactor_notes: Move methods between prototype and instance only after checking this binding and identity
Avoid subclassing refactors without tests for constructor/super order

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Subclasses extend behavior while relying on superclass initialization and methods.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: extends sets up prototype inheritance. Derived constructors must call super before using this. super.method resolves against the superclass prototype in method context.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: class D extends B { constructor(){ super(); } method(){ return super.method(); } }
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Subclass bugs often involve initialization order, method override contracts, and this/prototype expectations.
common_misuse: Using this before super
Breaking superclass invariants
Assuming super is a dynamic property read from this
tests_or_checks: Test constructor arguments and superclass invariants
safe_refactor_notes: Prefer composition if subclass contract is unclear
Do not reorder super and this initialization casually

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: CommonJS is Node’s historical module system built around require and module.exports.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: A CommonJS module exports by assigning to exports or module.exports and imports synchronously with require. Interop with ES modules depends on Node/tooling behavior that must be verified for the current runtime.

Mixing top-level import/export without config
Assuming named ES imports work from all CommonJS packages
tests_or_checks: Test import/require both sides if interop
safe_refactor_notes: Do not rewrite require to import without runtime/tool tests
Document interop adapters

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Map and Set are standard collection types for keys/values and unique membership.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: Map stores key-value associations with keys not limited to strings. Set stores unique values. WeakMap/WeakSet have object-key/value constraints and garbage-collection-oriented behavior.

Use WeakMap for private metadata tied to object lifetime
common_misuse: Using plain object as map with arbitrary user keys
Expecting JSON.stringify Map/Set to preserve entries
Using WeakMap when iteration is required
safe_refactor_notes: Switch object to Map only after updating access/serialization code
Keep conversion helpers at boundaries

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: JavaScript reports exceptional failures through thrown values, commonly Error objects.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: throw transfers control to nearest matching catch/finally. Error classes capture messages and, in many environments, stacks. Promise rejections are async error channels, not caught by surrounding synchronous try/catch unless awaited.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: throw new Error(msg); try { } catch (e) { } finally { }

Throwing inside async callback expecting outer try/catch
Ignoring Error object details
safe_refactor_notes: Do not change throw to return error without API contract update
Use finally for cleanup, not normal result substitution

language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: An iterable has a Symbol.iterator method returning an iterator. An iterator has next() returning {value, done}. Built-in collections and strings are iterable; plain objects are not iterable by default.

common_misuse: Using for/of on plain object
Assuming every array-like is iterable
Returning malformed next results

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Generator functions make it easier to define iterators and lazy sequences.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: function* returns a generator object. yield produces a value and pauses execution. return, throw, and delegation with yield* affect control flow between consumer and generator.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: function* g(){ yield x; } const it = g(); it.next(); yield* other

Ignoring return/throw path
Using generator where a simple array is clearer

safe_refactor_notes: Do not replace materialized arrays with generators without consumption tests
Document one-shot versus reusable iterable behavior

language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: A Promise settles once, either fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. then/catch/finally return promises and schedule handlers asynchronously according to the host event loop/microtask model.

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: async/await lets Promise-based code read like sequential code, while still returning promises.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: An async function always returns a Promise. await pauses the async function until the awaited value resolves or rejects. try/catch catches awaited rejections inside the async function, not unrelated async callbacks.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: async function f(){ const x = await p; return x; }

common_misuse: Forgetting that async function return value is a Promise
Awaiting operations sequentially that should run concurrently
Not awaiting a call whose rejection matters
debugging_symptoms: Caller receives Promise instead of value
safe_refactor_notes: Adding async to a function is API change unless callers already expect Promise
Preserve concurrency intentionally
